title: Birds Have 4 Cones, You Have 3. What Can't You See?
description:
Why can some animals see colors we can't even imagine? Your eyes have 3 color cones, while bees and many birds see ultraviolet, hummingbirds tell apart non-spectral colors like UV plus green, the mantis shrimp's 12 receptors turn out to be fast but not fine, and reindeer may spot dark lichen against UV-bright snow.

topic: Why can some animals see colors we can't even imagine?
script:
Hummingbirds see colors your brain has never made.
Not brighter colors, or sharper ones.
Whole new colors, with no names.
So how can an animal see a color we can't even imagine?
To find out, we have to start with you.
Light travels in waves of different lengths.
Your eyes catch a tiny slice of them,
from about 400 to 700 nanometers.
That slice is the rainbow,
violet at one end and red at the other.
Inside your eye are three kinds of color cells, called cones.
One likes blue light best, one likes green, and one likes red.
Every color you've ever seen,
is your brain comparing how hard those three are firing.
Yellow? That's your red and green cones firing together.
And here's a fun one.
Purple isn't in the rainbow at all.
When your red and blue cones fire, but green stays quiet,
your brain invents a color to fill the gap.
Scientists call that a non-spectral color.
Hold on to that idea.
Now take one cone away.
Dogs have just two, tuned to blue and yellow.
So a red ball on green grass,
looks to a dog like two similar, muddy shades.
Fewer cones, fewer colors.
So what happens with more?
Honeybees have three cones too, but they're shifted.
They see ultraviolet, blue and green.
Red? To a bee, red mostly looks dark.
Lots of flowers that look plain yellow to us,
have dark ultraviolet bullseyes in the middle.
They work like landing lights,
pointing the bee straight to the nectar.
Many birds go one step further.
They have four cone types, including one for ultraviolet.
Male and female blue tits look almost the same to us.
But in ultraviolet, the males' crowns shine brighter.
Now remember purple.
With three cones, you get one non-spectral color.
With four cones, there are way more ways to mix.
In 2020, scientists tested wild hummingbirds in the Rocky Mountains.
They lit up feeders with mixes like ultraviolet plus green.
And the birds learned to tell them apart from plain green.
That's a color you will never see.
It isn't greenish, or bluish.
It's something your brain has no slot for,
like trying to picture a brand new primary color.
So more cones always means more colors, right?
Meet the mantis shrimp.
It has around twelve kinds of color receptors.
For years, people said it must see a mind-blowing rainbow.
But in 2014, scientists actually tested it.
And it was worse than you at telling close shades apart.
Instead of comparing cones like we do,
it seems to read colors directly, like a barcode scanner.
Fast, but not fine.
So why bother seeing ultraviolet at all?
Take reindeer, out in the snowy Arctic.
Snow reflects ultraviolet, but their favorite food, lichen, soaks it up.
So scientists think lichen pops out as dark patches,
against the glowing snow.
Every animal sees the colors it needs to survive.
Your three cones are just one version of the world.
And somewhere, a hummingbird is looking at a flower,
in a color you'll never know.
Next up, what actually happens,
when a bee stings you?
key_facts: Humans see roughly 400-700 nm with 3 cone types (short/blue, medium/green, long/red)
Purple/magenta is a non-spectral color: the brain's mix of red and blue signals, not a single wavelength
Dogs have 2 cone types (blue and yellowish), so red and green look similar
Honeybees see ultraviolet, blue and green, and are not sensitive to red; many flowers have UV bullseye nectar guides
Many birds have 4 cone types including a UV/violet cone; blue tit males have more UV-reflective crowns
Stoddard et al. (Princeton, PNAS 2020) showed wild broad-tailed hummingbirds in the Rocky Mountains discriminate non-spectral colors such as UV+green
Mantis shrimp have about 12 color photoreceptor types but Thoen et al. (Science 2014) found poor discrimination of close colors; they appear to recognize colors directly
Reindeer eyes transmit UV; snow reflects UV while lichen absorbs it, so researchers think lichen stands out as dark
